# Solution

**Yes**, such a continuous surjective map exists.

## Construction

Consider the **degree-2 map** on the circle:
$$f : \mathbb{S}^1 \to \mathbb{S}^1, \quad f(z) = z^2.$$

This map is continuous and surjective: for any $w = e^{i\theta} \in \mathbb{S}^1$, the point $z = e^{i\theta/2}$ satisfies $f(z) = w$.

Define the map on the torus $T = \mathbb{S}^1 \times \mathbb{S}^1$ by:
$$g : T \to T, \quad g(z, w) = (z^2, w^2) = (f(z), f(w)).$$

## Verification

**Continuity and Surjectivity.** The map $g$ is continuous as a product of continuous maps. It is surjective: given $(a, b) \in T$, pick $z, w \in \mathbb{S}^1$ with $z^2 = a$ and $w^2 = b$ (possible by surjectivity of $f$), so $g(z,w) = (a,b)$.

**Induced map on $H_1$.** By the Künneth theorem, the first homology of the torus decomposes as:
$$H_1(T) \cong H_1(\mathbb{S}^1) \oplus H_1(\mathbb{S}^1) \cong \mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}.$$

Under this decomposition, the induced map of a product map $g = f \times f$ on $H_1$ is the direct sum of the induced maps of the factors:
$$g_* = f_* \oplus f_* : H_1(\mathbb{S}^1) \oplus H_1(\mathbb{S}^1) \to H_1(\mathbb{S}^1) \oplus H_1(\mathbb{S}^1).$$

The map $f(z) = z^2$ has **degree 2**, so $f_*$ is multiplication by 2 on $H_1(\mathbb{S}^1) \cong \mathbb{Z}$. Therefore:
$$g_*(a, b) = (2a, 2b) \quad \text{for all } (a,b) \in \mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}.$$

This is exactly multiplication by 2 on every element of $H_1(T)$. (The same conclusion holds for cohomology $H^1$, since $f^*$ on $H^1(\mathbb{S}^1)$ is also multiplication by 2.)

## Conclusion

The map $g(z,w) = (z^2, w^2)$ is a continuous surjective self-map of the torus whose induced homomorphism on $H_1$ multiplies every element by 2.
